**Given:** The Euclidean representation $V$, compact sphere compactification and exterior-multiplication convention in the statement.

[A1] AC is inherited from the bundle, Hilbert, Sobolev, Fredholm and sphere-cohomology suppliers. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The finite-chart calculus gives compact-manifold elliptic Fredholm realizations, parametrices, smooth kernels, Sobolev regularity, and principal-symbol composition and adjoints for finite-rank bundles. [[lem-equivariant-finite-chart-symbol-calculus]]

[F2] Controlled realization gives an additive representation-valued index on compact-support symbol classes, independent of compactification by excision, invariant under stabilized symbol homotopy and equivariant diffeomorphism, and compatible with group restriction and coefficient representations. On compact manifolds it is the kernel-minus-adjoint-kernel of an elliptic realization. No Bott normalization or embedding-index equality is assumed. [[lem-equivariant-controlled-symbol-realization]]

[F3] The associated-bundle product result, in particular its external-product special case followed by excision, makes the compact-support analytic index multiplicative under products of Euclidean open sets and their compact-support symbols. Its proof does not assume this normalization. [[lem-equivariant-associated-symbol-product-index]]

[F4] The de Rham groups of $S^m$ are one-dimensional in degrees $0,m$ and zero in other degrees for $m=1,2$. Integration of an exact top form on a compact oriented manifold without boundary is zero. [[thm-de-rham-cohomology-of-spheres]] [[thm-general-stokes-theorem]]

[F5] In the root convention the relative plane line symbol $z$ represents the generator $\beta=[\gamma]-1$, and its integer multiple is determined by boundary winding. [[thm-hopf-line-calculation-of-k-zero-of-the-two-sphere]]



**Given:** The data and index interfaces above. All symbol deformations below have one common compact support for their failure of invertibility.

1.1 Exterior multiplication satisfies $\varepsilon_z^2=0$ and $\varepsilon_z\varepsilon_z^*+\varepsilon_z^*\varepsilon_z=|z|^2I$: verify first for an orthonormal basis and use bilinearity. Hence the stated square identity and compact-support class hold. Under $V=V_1\oplus V_2$, the exterior-algebra identification gives $k_{V}(z_1,z_2)=k_{V_1}(z_1)\widehat\otimes1+1\widehat\otimes k_{V_2}(z_2)$. This is exactly the graded symbol product, with no extra sign. Thus $b_{V_1\oplus V_2}=b_{V_1}\boxtimes b_{V_2}$, equivariantly for any group preserving the decomposition. For a real orthogonal bundle the real metric extends complex-bilinearly to identify its complexification with its complex dual. The same doubled-real Bott convention can therefore be written with the dual, while such an identification is not asserted for arbitrary complex bundles. [given, construct, algebra]

1.2 We first fix the nonequivariant line sign explicitly. On $S^1=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$ let $P_+$ project onto $e^{inx}$, $n\ge0$, and put $A=e^{ix}P_++1-P_+$. The Fejér kernels show that trigonometric polynomials are dense in $L^2$: they approximate continuous functions uniformly, and continuous functions approximate interval indicators and hence simple functions in $L^2$. Thus the Fourier vectors are a complete orthonormal basis. The map $A$ sends the $n$th vector to the $(n+1)$st for $n\ge0$ and to itself for $n<0$. Its images are exactly all nonzero modes, orthonormally, so $\ker A=0$, its range is closed and its cokernel is the constants. Its index is $-1$. To check its actual symbol, localize with a smooth function $f$ in an interval of length less than $2\pi$. The local symbol of $P_+$ is $(2\pi)^{-1}\sum_{n\ge0}\widehat f(n-\xi)e^{ix(n-\xi)}$. For $\xi\to-\infty$ this and every derivative decrease faster than every power, by rapid decay of the Fourier transform of $f$. For $\xi\to+\infty$ subtract the rapidly decreasing sum over $n<0$ from the full Fourier reconstruction $f(x)$. The resulting estimates, also off the diagonal, prove that $P_+$ is classical of order zero with leading symbol $1$ on $\xi>0$ and $0$ on $\xi<0$. Thus $A$ has symbol $e^{ix}$ on the positive ray and $1$ on the negative ray. [A1, F1, F2, construct, algebra]

1.3 The compact de Rham operator has index its cohomological Euler representation, as follows directly from [F1]. On a compact invariant Riemannian manifold let $D=d+d^*$, acting from even to odd complex forms, with the usual group action on forms. Integration by parts gives $D^2=\Delta=dd^*+d^*d$ and $\langle\Delta u,u\rangle=\|du\|^2+\|d^*u\|^2$. The principal symbol of $D$ is $i(\varepsilon_\xi-\varepsilon_\xi^*)$, so it is elliptic. The parametrix and regularity give smooth finite-dimensional kernels and closed range; since the self-adjoint elliptic $\Delta$ has cokernel its kernel, its restriction to the orthogonal complement of its kernel is invertible, with inverse $G$ improving Sobolev order by two. For closed smooth $\alpha$ write $\alpha=h+\Delta G\alpha$. Commutation $d\Delta=\Delta d$ shows $dG\alpha$ is harmonic; it is exact, so its norm vanishes by integration by parts against its primitive. Hence $\alpha=h+dd^*G\alpha$. A harmonic exact form is zero by the same norm calculation. Thus harmonic forms identify with cohomology, equivariantly because all operations commute with the compact action. This proves the stated index comparison here without invoking a scalar Hodge assertion for a matrix complex. [F1, F2, construct, algebra]

2.1 Homotope the loop $e^{ix}$ to $e^{i\varphi(x)}$, where $\varphi$ rises smoothly from $0$ to $2\pi$ inside a proper coordinate interval and is constant near the ends; the homotopy is $e^{i((1-t)x+t\varphi(x))}$. It is smooth periodic, including at the cut, and preserves symbol invertibility on both rays. The final symbol is extended from the interval. On its cotangent plane a representative is $1+(e^{i\varphi(x)}-1)h(\xi)$, where $h=0$ for $\xi\le-1$ and $h=1$ for $\xi\ge1$. Its only possible zeros lie in a compact rectangle. On the rectangle it is $e^{i\varphi(x)}$ on the top and $1$ elsewhere. With orientation $dx\wedge d\xi$, the top is traversed right to left, so its winding is $-1$. More explicitly its boundary loop divided by $\bar z$ on a disk has winding zero and a continuous logarithm, so a logarithm homotopy identifies it with $\bar z$. The loops $z\oplus\bar z$ contract to a constant invertible matrix through $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}t z&-\sqrt{1-t^2}\\\sqrt{1-t^2}&t\bar z\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ for $1\ge t\ge0$. Consequently this relative class is $-b_{\mathbb R}$. By symbol homotopy, excision and step 1.2, $a_{\{1\}}(b_{\mathbb R})=1$. This establishes the sign independently of de Rham dimensions. [F2, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

2.2 We next prove a symbol identity on $S^m=\mathbb R^m\cup\{\infty\}$, for $m=1,2$, equivariantly under $O(m)$ acting on the first $m$ coordinates. Identify the two closed hemispheres with the unit disks by $x\mapsto(2x/(1+|x|^2),\pm(1-|x|^2)/(1+|x|^2))$. On their boundary the tangent trivializations differ by $h_x=I-2xx^{\mathsf T}$: differentiating the two maps gives exactly this relation. The conformal Euclidean frames have the same positive scale on the equator. Use the metric to identify tangent and cotangent fibers, with transition $h_x$; the exterior algebra then has transition $\Lambda h_x$. The de Rham symbol is equivalent to the Koszul symbol of $\xi$: the diagonal unitary on degree $k$ given by $i^k$ conjugates $\varepsilon_\xi+\varepsilon_\xi^*$ to $i(\varepsilon_\xi-\varepsilon_\xi^*)$. Positive conformal factors in $\xi$ can be homotoped to one while preserving invertibility outside the zero section. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.3, construct, algebra]

3.1 In these two disk trivializations deform the Koszul differential respectively to exterior multiplication by $\xi-isx$ and by $\xi+isx$, $0\le s\le1$, and take differential plus Hermitian adjoint. Since $h_xx=-x$ on $|x|=1$, these vectors agree under the transition $h_x$, so the deformation is a globally defined $O(m)$-equivariant symbol. Its square is $(|\xi|^2+s^2|x|^2)I$. Thus throughout the deformation its noninvertibility lies in the compact zero section, and at $s=1$ it is confined to the centers of the two disks. The disk charts have corners only as a decomposition; the glued symbols are continuous and can be smoothed relatively near the two centers without changing their class, as follows: the leading linear-in-$\xi$ part is already the original smooth elliptic symbol, and only the bounded base-dependent perturbation needs smoothing. Its norm is bounded uniformly in $s$, so outside one fixed fiber radius the unchanged leading part dominates. Inside that radius, and outside small fixed pole neighborhoods at the final parameter, compactness gives a positive least singular value. Local convolutions and an invariant partition of unity approximate the perturbation by less than half this value, fixing the original symbol at $s=0$ and fixing its prescribed form near the poles. Average over $O(m)$; convexity preserves the same approximation bound. Straight-line interpolation then preserves invertibility on that complement. This constructs a smooth representative of the same continuous compact-support homotopy. After splitting into the two disjoint pole neighborhoods, multiplying the upper vector by $i$ changes it to $x+i\xi$; multiplying the lower by $i$ changes it to $-x+i\xi$, and multiplication by $-1$ changes that to $x-i\xi$. Each scalar multiplication is joined to the identity through unit complex scalars and therefore preserves the class and its support. Write $\vartheta(x,\xi)=(x,-\xi)$ and let $j_0,j_\infty$ denote open extension from these two pole charts. The actual compact symbol identity is consequently $[\sigma(D_{S^m})]=j_0b_{\mathbb R^m}+j_\infty\vartheta^*b_{\mathbb R^m}$. This is an explicit full-symbol support homotopy with the two pole signs fixed. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

4.1 The sphere map interchanging the two hemispheres is $O(m)$-equivariant and carries their chosen tangent coordinates into one another. Excision and diffeomorphism covariance therefore give $a_{O(m)}(\sigma(D_{S^m}))=a_{O(m)}(b_{\mathbb R^m})+a_{O(m)}(\vartheta^*b_{\mathbb R^m})$. For $m=1$ let $\epsilon$ be the nontrivial character of $O(1)$. The class identity $\vartheta^*b_{\mathbb R}=-\epsilon b_{\mathbb R}$ is explicit. On the unit complex circle the direct sum on the left of $\vartheta^*b+\epsilon b=0$ has domain $1\oplus\epsilon$ and, after exchanging target summands, matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&z\\\bar z&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The path $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\sin t&\cos t\,z\\\cos t\,\bar z&-\sin t\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $0\le t\le\pi/2$, is equivariant for the involution $z\mapsto-z$ and the matrix representation $\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$, is invertible since its determinant is $-1$, and ends at a constant equivariant isomorphism. Hence the sum is zero as a relative class. For $m=2$ restricted to $SO(2)$, $\vartheta$ is properly equivariantly homotopic to the identity by $(x,\xi)\mapsto(x,R_{\pi t}\xi)$; on the symbols its square norm remains $|x|^2+|\xi|^2$. Thus $\vartheta^*b=b$ for this group. [F2, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 On the circle, constants generate $H^0$ and $dx$ generates $H^1$; reflection acts by $1$ and $-1$, respectively. Hence step 1.3 gives $a_{O(1)}(\sigma(D_{S^1}))=1-\epsilon$. If $r=a_{O(1)}(b_{\mathbb R})=u+v\epsilon$, step 4.1 gives $(1-\epsilon)r=1-\epsilon$, or $u-v=1$. Restriction to the trivial group and step 2.1 give $u+v=1$. Thus $u=1,v=0$: this is the full $O(1)$ representation, not just its dimension. On $S^2$, [F4] gives only $H^0$ and $H^2$; the invariant area form has nonzero integral and is therefore not exact, so it generates the latter group. Both representations are trivial under rotations. Thus $a_{SO(2)}(\sigma(D_{S^2}))=2$. Step 4.1 implies $2a_{SO(2)}(b_{\mathbb R^2})=2$. Every unitary circle representation splits into weight spaces; integer weight multiplicities make its representation group torsion-free. Consequently $a_{SO(2)}(b_{\mathbb R^2})=1$ as a representation. [F2, F4, step 2.1, step 1.3, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Every orthogonal matrix $Q$ on $V$ admits an orthogonal decomposition into invariant real lines with eigenvalue $+1$ or $-1$, and real planes on which it is a rotation: diagonalize its complex unitary complexification and pair conjugate eigenvectors; real eigenvectors span the remaining $\pm1$ spaces. Thus $Q$ belongs to a block subgroup $H$ which is a product of copies of $O(1)$ and $SO(2)$. On restriction to this entire subgroup, step 1.1 identifies $b_V$ with the product of the line and plane symbols. By [F3] and step 5.1 its index is $1\in R(H)$. Restriction of a Fredholm index simply restricts its finite kernel representations, so the character of $a_{O(n)}(b_V)$ takes the value $1$ at the original arbitrary matrix $Q$. This proves equality of characters on every component of $O(n)$, including orientation-reversing matrices. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

7.1 Equality of these characters implies equality in $R(O(n))$. Indeed average inner products over $O(n)$ to make representations unitary, and take invariant orthogonal complements to decompose them into irreducibles. Normalized invariant volume on $O(n)$ can be obtained from the bi-invariant metric induced by the trace inner product on its skew-symmetric matrices, giving equal mass to its two components. Averaging on $\operatorname{Hom}(U,W)$ is the orthogonal projection onto intertwining maps, so the integral of $\overline{\chi_U}\chi_W$ is their dimension; for irreducibles this is $1$ if isomorphic and $0$ otherwise, by Schur's lemma (an eigenvalue of an intertwiner and its invariant kernel prove that lemma over $\mathbb C$). Pairing a zero virtual character against every irreducible therefore gives zero multiplicities. Apply this to step 6.1 minus the trivial character to obtain $a_{O(n)}(b_V)=1$. For $n=0$ the open Euclidean set is a point and its symbol is the even line, whose index is directly $1$. Group restriction and coefficient tensoring in [F2] give the general assertion. Finally the complex orientation is the ordered product $dx_1\wedge d\xi_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_n\wedge d\xi_n$, whereas $(d\theta)^n/n!$ is its $(-1)^n$ multiple, proving the exact orientation convention. [F2, step 1.1, step 6.1, construct, algebra] ∎



This proof normalizes the compact analytic symbol index. It does not assume an analytic–topological index comparison or a normal embedding compatibility theorem. Its use of de Rham operators is limited to the explicitly computed line and rotation-plane tests; products and character detection establish the full orthogonal-group conclusion.

**Given:** The circle, trivial geometric $G$-action, coefficient representation $V$, and Fourier convention $e^{inx}$ in the example.

[A1] AC is inherited from the bundle, Sobolev and Fredholm suppliers. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Smooth classical symbols with the positive Fourier kernel $e^{i(x-y)\xi}$ have the local symbol calculus and Sobolev/Fredholm properties specified by the finite-chart supplier. [[lem-equivariant-finite-chart-symbol-calculus]]

[F2] The compact symbol index is invariant under stabilized symbol homotopy, equals the Fredholm kernel difference of a realization, is compatible with coefficient representations, and is independent of compactification for controlled compact-support representatives. [[lem-equivariant-controlled-symbol-realization]]

[F3] The relative plane symbol clutched by $z$ represents $\beta=[\gamma]-1$ in the fixed root convention; a loop of winding $k$ represents $k\beta$. [[thm-hopf-line-calculation-of-k-zero-of-the-two-sphere]]



**Given:** The preceding data and symbol/index conventions.

1.1 The exponentials are an orthonormal complete system. Completeness can be checked without an additional spectral theorem: convolution of a continuous periodic function with the Fejér kernel is a trigonometric polynomial and converges uniformly, since the nonnegative kernel has integral one and its mass outside each neighborhood of zero tends to zero; continuous functions are dense in $L^2$ by approximation of interval indicators and simple functions. Thus an $L^2$ function orthogonal to every exponential is zero. Consequently $P_+$ is a norm-one orthogonal projection. On Fourier basis vectors, $A(e^{inx}v)=e^{i(n+1)x}v$ for $n\ge0$ and $A(e^{inx}v)=e^{inx}v$ for $n<0$. These images are exactly the distinct nonzero modes, so $A$ is an isometry onto their closed span, its kernel is zero, and its cokernel is the constants. Every identification commutes with $G$, proving $\operatorname{Ind}_G(A)=-[V]$. [A1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 To verify the actual classical symbol, let $f$ be a smooth cutoff supported in a coordinate interval of length less than $2\pi$, and extend it by zero to $\mathbb R$. With $\widehat f(\eta)=\int e^{-ix\eta}f(x)\,dx$, local application to $f(x)e^{ix\xi}$ gives $e^{-ix\xi}P_+(fe^{i(\cdot)\xi})(x)=(2\pi)^{-1}\sum_{n\ge0}\widehat f(n-\xi)e^{ix(n-\xi)}$. Every derivative of $\widehat f$ decays faster than every power, by repeated integration by parts. For $\xi\to-\infty$ the sum and all its $x,\xi$ derivatives are rapidly decreasing, since $n-\xi\ge n+|\xi|$. For $\xi\to+\infty$ use full Fourier reconstruction, whose sum is $f(x)$ on the chosen chart, and subtract the sum over $n<0$; that sum has the same rapid estimates. Uniform bounds on the remaining compact $\xi$ interval follow by convergence of the differentiated sums. Hence this localized complete symbol has leading term $f(x)$ on the positive ray and zero on the negative ray, with smooth rapidly decreasing remainders away from a bounded frequency interval. Off the diagonal the localized kernels are smooth by the same integration-by-parts estimates. This establishes $P_+$ in the calculus [F1], with the asserted two-ray symbol. Multiplication by $e^{ix}$ gives the displayed elliptic symbol of $A$. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Choose a smooth real function $\varphi$ on $[0,2\pi]$, equal to $0$ near $0$, equal to $2\pi$ near $2\pi$, and increasing only in a proper interior interval $I$. The loops $u_t(x)=\exp(i((1-t)x+t\varphi(x)))$ are smooth periodic degree-one loops, for $0\le t\le1$, joining $e^{ix}$ to a loop equal to $1$ outside $I$. All derivatives match at the endpoints because $\varphi$ is constant there. On the positive cotangent ray replace $e^{ix}$ by $u_t(x)$, leaving the negative symbol $1$. These are elliptic symbol homotopies; [F2] preserves their index. At $t=1$ the symbol is the identity outside the compact subinterval where $\varphi$ varies, and its class is extended from $T^*I$. A coordinate on $I$ gives the following compact representative on $\mathbb R^2$: $a(x,\xi)=1+(e^{i\varphi(x)}-1)h(\xi)$, where $h=0$ on $\xi\le-1$, $h=1$ on $\xi\ge1$, and $\varphi$ is extended by its endpoint constants. Its possible zeros lie in a compact rectangle, and its boundary values are $e^{i\varphi(x)}$ on the top and $1$ on the other three sides. [F2, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Traverse that rectangle counterclockwise in the coordinate orientation $dx\wedge d\xi$. On the top $x$ decreases, so the change of argument is $-2\pi$. The boundary map has winding $-1$, whereas $x+i\xi$ has winding $+1$. Their class identity can also be seen directly: map the rectangle to a disk; the ratio of its boundary function to $\bar z$ has winding zero and hence a continuous logarithm (integrate its logarithmic derivative and use the zero total integral). Exponentiating scalar multiples of that logarithm gives a homotopy to $\bar z$. The sum of the $z$ and $\bar z$ relative symbols is zero: the boundary matrices $\operatorname{diag}(z,\bar z)$ contract through $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}t z&-\sqrt{1-t^2}\\\sqrt{1-t^2}&t\bar z\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $1\ge t\ge0$, to a constant invertible matrix, and then to the identity. Thus $[a]=-b$, consistently with [F3]. Tensoring the argument by $V$ proves the class assertion. Since $a$ has index $-[V]$ by steps 1.1 and 3.1, additivity and excision give $a_{\{1\}}(b)=1$, where $a$ denotes the compact-support analytic index. Finally $d\theta=d\xi\wedge dx$ reverses the chosen complex orientation, giving precisely the orientation statement in the example. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎



The geometric action on the circle is trivial here. Multiplication by $e^{ix}$ does not commute with geometric circle rotations on the same source and target bundle, so this operator does not supply a rotation-equivariant Hardy index. The coefficient-representation statement is the equivariant assertion used here.
